## Introduction 

### 🎯 Lecture Goals {-}

In this lecture, we’ll tackle three key questions:

* **How** do $\mathrm{p}$-values actually work?
* **What** are the typical misuses and misinterpretations of $\mathrm{p}$-values?
* **What** is good practice when working with $\mathrm{p}$-values?

We’ll explore these questions using the **two-sided $t$-test** as our main example. Parallel arguments apply to one-sided testing and other hypothesis tests (F-test, etc.); see @sec-OtherTests.

```{r}
#| echo: false
library("scales")
library("extraDistr")

value <- 0
value <- value + 1
set.seed(33)
n     <- 5
Y_1   <- round(rnorm(n, mean = 5), 2)
Y_2   <- round(rnorm(n, mean = 5), 2)
X     <- round(Y_2 - Y_1, 2)
X_bar <- round(mean(X), 2)
s     <- round(sd(X),   2)
T_obs <- round((sqrt(n) * X_bar)/s, 2)
```

-------------------------------------------------

### 💻 Example: Marketing Campaign {-}

Imagine a company runs a marketing campaign in $n = 5$ stores and measures sales *before* and *after* the campaign.

<br>

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Data Table


Store | Sales Before | Sales After | Difference (After $-$ Before)
----|------------|------------|--------- 
$1$   |$`r format(Y_1[1], nsmall=2)`$|$`r format(Y_2[1], nsmall=2)`$|$X_{1,\mathrm{obs}}=`r format(X[1], nsmall=2)`$
$2$   |$`r format(Y_1[2], nsmall=2)`$|$`r format(Y_2[2], nsmall=2)`$|$X_{2,\mathrm{obs}}=`r format(X[2], nsmall=2)`$
$3$   |$`r format(Y_1[3], nsmall=2)`$|$`r format(Y_2[3], nsmall=2)`$|$X_{3,\mathrm{obs}}=`r format(X[3], nsmall=2)`$
$4$   |$`r format(Y_1[4], nsmall=2)`$|$`r format(Y_2[4], nsmall=2)`$|$X_{4,\mathrm{obs}}=`r format(X[4], nsmall=2)`$
$5$   |$`r format(Y_1[5], nsmall=2)`$|$`r format(Y_2[5], nsmall=2)`$|$X_{5,\mathrm{obs}}=`r format(X[5], nsmall=2)`$  

## Data Plot

@fig-diffData visualizes the observed differences $X_{i,\mathrm{obs}},$ $i=1,\dots,5.$

<br>

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig.height: 0.75
#| out.width: "1\\textwidth"
#| fig-align: center
#| label: fig-diffData
#| fig-cap: "Sales differences (sales after minus before the marketing campaign)."
par(mar = c(2, 0, 0, 0))
plot(x = X, y = rep(0.002, n), 
     pch = 21, 
     col = alpha("red", 0.5), 
     bg  = alpha("red", 0.5), 
     cex = 2, axes = FALSE, 
     ylab = "", xlab = "", xlim = c(-2.1,2.1), ylim = c(0,.005), yaxs="i")
axis(1, at = -2:2, cex.axis = 1.5, lwd = 2, family="serif", pos =0)
```
:::

**We want to know:**

* **Research question:**  </br> 
Is there a marketing effect? Did it show a tendency (location-shift) toward *significantly* higher or lower sales?

* **Statistical question:** </br> 
Is the mean, $\mu,$ of $X_1,\dots,X_n$ different from zero?


::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
## Assumption
There are no systematic differences (mean-shifts) between sales before and after the marketing campaign, other than the potential impact of the campaign itself.
:::

-------------------------------------------------

#### **Two-Sided $t$-Test** {-}
We test

<center>
$\displaystyle H_0\colon \mu = 0 \quad$ versus $\displaystyle \quad H_1\colon \mu \neq 0$
</center>

<br>

The $t$-statistic is
$$
\mathrm{T} = \frac{\bar{X} - 0}{S/\sqrt{n}}\overset{H_0}{\sim} t_{n-1},
$$
where 

* $n$ is the sample size,
* $\bar{X}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$ is the **sample mean**, and
* $S= \sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar{X})}$ is the **sample standard deviation.**

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal" collapse="true"}
## Assumptions underlying the $t$-test
* Random (iid) sample: 
$X_1,\dots,X_n\overset{\operatorname{iid}}{\sim}X$ 
* For small $n$: 
$X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ 
* For large $n$: we just need finite mean $E(X)=\mu$ and variance $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$ (Central Limit Theorem helps).
:::


-------------------------------------------------



#### **Observed (obs) Value of the $t$-Statistic (Marketing Example)** {-}

$$
\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}} = \frac{\bar{X}_{\mathrm{obs}} - 0}{S_{\mathrm{obs}}/\sqrt{n}} = `r format(T_obs, nsmall=2)`
$$ 

* $n=5$
* $\bar{X}_{\mathrm{obs}}=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{i=1}^5 X_{i,\mathrm{obs}} = `r format(X_bar,nsmall=2)`$ 
* $S_{\mathrm{obs}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{5-1}\sum_{i=1}^5(X_{i,\mathrm{obs}}-\bar{X}_{\mathrm{obs}})} = `r format(s,nsmall=2)`$ 

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal" collapse="true"}
## Computing $\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}$ in `R`

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
X_obs <- c(0.64, -0.72, -0.23, 0.91, 1.06)
n     <- length(X_obs)
X_bar <- mean(X_obs)
S_obs <- sd(X_obs)

## Observed t-statistic
T_obs <- (X_bar - 0)/(S_obs/sqrt(n))

## Alternatively: 
result <- t.test(x           = X_obs, 
                 mu          = 0, 
                 alternative = "two.sided")
T_obs  <- result$statistic
```
:::

#### **Test Decision using Critical Values (Marketing Example)** {-}


::: {.panel-tabset}

## Test Decision

Critical values of the $t_{n-1}$-distribution (significance level $\alpha = 0.05$):

<center>
$\mathrm{q}_{\alpha/2} = `r round(qt(p = 0.05/2, df=4), 2)`\;$ and $\;\mathrm{q}_{1-\alpha/2} = `r round(qt(p = 1-0.05/2, df=4), 2)`$

```{r}

n     <- 5
alpha <- 0.05
qt(p =     alpha/2, df = n-1)
qt(p = 1 - alpha/2, df = n-1)
```

## The Two-Sided $\mathrm{p}$-Value of the $t$-Test 


### ⚙️ Definition of the $\mathrm{p}$-Value {-}

<!-- 
::: {.panel-tabset}
## Definition 
-->


::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
## General Definition of the $\mathrm{p}$-Value 
The $\mathrm{p}$-value, $\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}},$ is the probability of obtaining realizations of the test statistic $\mathrm{T}$ **at least as extreme as** the one realization computed from the data $(\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}})$ — assuming that $H_0$ is true.


By **extreme,** we mean extreme *in the direction(s) of the alternative hypothesis.*
:::

**Two-sided $\mathrm{p}$-value of the $t$-test** 
$$\displaystyle\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} = \mathrm{P}\big(\,|\mathrm{T}|\,\geq |\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\;\big|\;H_0\;\text{is true}\big)$$

### 🧮 Computing the $\mathrm{p}$-Value {-}

::: {.panel-tabset}
## Null Distribution
Note that 
$$
\mathrm{T}=\frac{\bar{X}-0}{S/\sqrt{n}}\overset{H_0}{\sim}t_{n-1}\phantom{Half}
$$
implies that 
<!-- the [**absolute value** $|\mathrm{T}|$]{style="background-color: yellow; padding: 0.1em 0.1em;"} of the random $t$-statistic is Half-$t_{n-1}$ distributed, -->
$$
\highlight{|\mathrm{T}|}=\frac{|\bar{X}-0|}{S/\sqrt{n}}\overset{H_0}{\sim}\highlight{\textrm{Half-}t_{n-1}.}
$$

## Density Function

<!-- # "Densities functions of the null-distribution $t_{\\operatorname{df}}$ of $\\mathrm{T}$ and $\\textrm{Half-}t_{\\operatorname{df}}$ of $|\\mathrm{T}|$ with $\\operatorname{df}=n-1=4$ (marketing example)." -->


```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig.height: 3
#| out.width: "1\\textwidth"
#| fig-align: center
#| label: fig-Halft
#| fig-cap: The density function of the Half-$t_{n-1}$ distribution is the folded version of the density function of the $t_{n-1}$ distribution.

library("extraDistr")

alpha  <- 0.05
df     <- 5-1
q_1    <- -abs(T_obs)
q_2    <- abs(T_obs)

p_obs <- round(2 * min(pt(q_1, df = df), pt(q_2, df = df)), 2)

xx0    <- seq(0.00001, 5, len=100)
##
xx1    <- seq(-5, q_1, len=25)
yy1    <- dt(x = xx1, df = df)
##
xx2    <- seq(q_2,  5, len=25)
yy2    <- dt(x = xx2, df = df)
##
xx3    <- seq(abs(T_obs),  5, len=25)
yy3    <- dht(x = xx3, nu = df)

par(mar = c(4.5, .1, .5, .1), family = "serif")
plot(y = dht(x = xx0, nu = df), x = xx0,
      xlab = "", ylab = "", main = "",
      lwd = 2, col = 1, xlim = c(-5, 5),
      xaxs="i",yaxs="i", axes = FALSE, type="l")
polygon(x = c(xx1,rev(xx1)), y=c(yy1, rep(0,length(yy1))), border = NA, col = gray(.95))
polygon(x = c(xx2,rev(xx2)), y=c(yy2, rep(0,length(yy2))), border = NA, col = gray(.95))
curve(expr = dt(x = x, df = df), lwd = 2, col = gray(.75), add = TRUE)
polygon(x = c(xx3,rev(xx3)), y=c(yy3, rep(0,length(yy3))), border = NA, col = myRed)
lines(x=c(0,0), y = c(0,dht(x = xx0, nu = df)[1]), lwd=2)
lines(y = dht(x = xx0, nu = df), x = xx0, lwd = 2, col = 1)
lines(x=c(0,0), y = c(0,dht(x = xx0, nu = df)[1]), lwd=2)
axis(1, cex.axis = 1.5, family = "serif")
axis(1, at =  T_obs, col = "red", labels = FALSE, tck=-0.11)
#axis(1, at = -T_obs, col = gray(.75), labels = FALSE, tck=-0.11)
mtext(side = 1, text = expression("|"~T[obs]~"|"), at = c(abs(T_obs)), line = 3.5, cex = 1.5, family = "serif")
legend("topright", pch=22, cex=1.5, 
       col = myRed, 
       legend=c(bquote(p[obs]==.(p_obs))), 
       bty="n", pt.bg = myRed, title = "")

legend("topleft", lty = 1, lwd=2, col=c(1, gray(.75)),
        legend=c(expression(f[paste("Half-",italic(t)["n-1"])]),expression(f[paste(italic(t)["n-1"])])),#c(expression(paste("Half-",italic(t)[n-1])), expression(italic(t)[n-1])), 
        bty="n", cex = 1.5, title = "Density Functions")       
```


## Distribution Function
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{F}_{\,\text{Half-}t_{n-1}}(x)&=\mathrm{P}(|\textrm{T}|\leq x\mid H_0\;\text{is true}),\quad |\textrm{T}|\overset{H_0}{\sim} \textrm{Half-}t_{n-1}
\end{align*}

<center> 
$\mathrm{F}_{\,\text{Half-}t_{n-1}}(x) =$ `extraDistr::pht(q = x, nu = n - 1)`
</center>

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig.height: 2.5
#| out.width: "1\\textwidth"
#| fig-align: center
#| label: fig-CDFHalft
#| fig-cap: "Distribution function of the null-distribution $\\textrm{Half-}t_{\\operatorname{df}}$ with $\\operatorname{df}=n-1=4$ (marketing example)."

library("extraDistr")

alpha  <- 0.05
df     <- 5-1

par(mar = c(2.5, 2.5, .5, .1), family = "serif")
plot(y = pht(q = xx0, nu = df), x = xx0,
      xlab = "", ylab = "", main = "",
      lwd = 2, col = 1, xlim = c(0, 4.125), ylim = c(0, 1.25),
      xaxs="i",yaxs="i", axes = FALSE, type="l")
abline(h=1, lty=3)
axis(1, cex.axis = 1.5, family = "serif", at = seq(0,4.5,by=1))
axis(2, cex.axis = 1.5, family = "serif", at = seq(0,1,by=0.5))
legend("right", lty = 1, lwd=2, col=1,
        legend=expression(F[paste("Half-",italic(t)["n-1"])]), 
        bty="n", cex = 1.5, title = "Distribution Function")
```

:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
## Computing the $\mathrm{p}$-Value of the Two-Sided $t$-Test

<!-- 
<br>
The distribution function $\mathrm{F}_{\,\text{Half-}t_{n-1}}(x)$ of the Half-$t_{n-1}$ distribution allows us to compute the $\mathrm{p}$-value, $\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}},$ for the two-sided $t$-statistic $|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|$: 
-->

\begin{align*}
\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} 
& = \mathrm{P}\big(\,|\mathrm{T}|\,\geq |\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\;\big|\;H_0\;\text{is true}\big)\\[1ex]
& = 1 - \mathrm{P}\big(\highlight{|\mathrm{T}|}\leq |\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\;\big|\highlight{H_0\;\text{is true}}\big)\\[1ex]
& = 1 - \highlight{\mathrm{F}_{\,\text{Half-}t_{n-1}}}\big(|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\big)
\end{align*}
:::

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### **Computing the $\mathrm{p}$-Value (Marketing Example)** {-}

\begin{align*}
\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}
&=1 - \mathrm{F}_{\,\text{Half-}t_{n-1}}\big(|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\big)\\
&=1 - \mathrm{F}_{\,\text{Half-}t_{n-1}}\big(\,`r abs(T_obs)`\,\big)=`r p_obs`
\end{align*}

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Plot

Computation of the observed $\operatorname{p}$-value:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig.height: 2.5
#| out.width: "1\\textwidth"
#| fig-align: center

library("extraDistr")
n  <- 5
df <- n - 1

## 1 minus the distribution function of the Half-t
p_obs <- 1 - pht(q = abs(T_obs), nu = df)


alpha  <- 0.05
df     <- 5-1

myfun <- function(x){1-pht(q = x, nu = df)}

par(mar = c(4.5, 9, 1, 0.5), family = "serif")
curve(expr = myfun,
      xlab = "", ylab = "", main = "",
      lwd = 2, col = 1, xlim = c(0, 4),
      ylim = c(0, 1), xaxs="i",yaxs="i", axes = FALSE)
axis(1, cex.axis = 1.5, family = "serif", mgp = c(3, 1, 0))
axis(2, at = c(0,1), labels = c("0","1"), cex.axis = 1.5, family = "serif", las=2, mgp = c(3, 1, 0))
axis(1, at =  T_obs, col = "blue", labels = FALSE, tck=-0.15)
axis(2, at =  myfun(T_obs), col = "blue", labels = FALSE, tck=-0.05)
lines(x = c(0,T_obs), y= rep(myfun(T_obs), 2), col="blue")
lines(x = rep(T_obs, 2), y= c(0, myfun(T_obs)), col="blue")
##
mtext(side = 1, text = bquote("|"~T[obs]~"|"==.(T_obs)), at = c(abs(T_obs)), line = 3.5, cex = 1.5, family = "serif")
corners = par("usr") #Gets the four corners of plot area (x1, x2, y1, y2)
par(xpd = TRUE) #Draw outside plot area
text(x = corners[1]-.75, y = mean(myfun(T_obs)), bquote(p[obs]==.(round(myfun(T_obs), 2))), srt = 0, cex = 1.5, family = "serif")

legend("top", lty = 1, lwd=2,
       legend=expression(1-F[paste("Half-",italic(t)["n-1"])]),
       bty="n", cex = 1.5)
```


## `R`-Codes

Computation of the observed $\operatorname{p}$-value:
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
library("extraDistr")
n  <- 5
df <- n - 1

## 1 minus the distribution function of the Half-t
p_obs <- 1 - pht(q = abs(T_obs), nu = df)

## Alternatively: 
result <- t.test(X_obs, mu = 0, alternative = "two.sided")
p_obs  <- result$p.value
```
:::

-------------------------------------------------

### ⚖️ Test Decision based on the $\mathrm{p}$-Value {-}

<br>

* We **reject** $H_0$ at the significance level $0<\alpha<1$ if 
$$
\highlight{\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} < \alpha}
$$

* We **fail to reject** $H_0$ at the significance level $0<\alpha<1$ if 
$$
\highlight{\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} \geq \alpha}
$$


Usual significance levels: $\alpha=0.05$ or $\alpha=0.01.$

-------------------------------------------------

#### **Test Decision (Marketing Example)** {-}

Since 
$$
\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}=`r round(p_obs,2)` \geq \alpha = 0.05
$$
we **fail to reject** $H_0\colon \mu =0$ at the significance level $\alpha=0.05.$ 

<!-- We also fail to reject $H_0$ at any other typically used significance level such as, for instance, $\alpha=0.1$ or $\alpha=0.01.$  -->


::: {.callout-caution icon="false" appearance="minimal"}
## ⚠️ Failing to reject $H_0$ does not mean that $H_0$ is true! (See @sec-MissUses.)

<!-- 
<br>
Failing to reject $H_0$ only means that a potential impact of the marketing campaign is not large enough to stand out from the random variation captured by the standard error $(S_{\mathrm{obs}}/\sqrt{n});$ see @sec-MissUses.

* "Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence." [@Sagan_1997].
* [Argument from ignorance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argument_from_ignorance) 
-->

:::

<!-- 
### 🤝 $\mathrm{p}$-Values vs Critical Values {-}

$\mathrm{p}$-values and critical values lead to exactly **equivalent test decisions:**


|                         | Reject $H_0$                        | Fail to Reject $H_0$|
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------|------------------------|
|**$\mathrm{p}$-Values:** |$\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\,<\alpha$ |$\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\, \geq \alpha$|
|**Critical Values:**  |$|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}| > \mathrm{q}_{1-\alpha}$ |$|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}| \leq  \mathrm{q}_{1-\alpha}$|

> With $\mathrm{q}_{1-\alpha}$ denoting the $(1-\alpha)$-quantile of the Half-$t_{n-1}$ distribution.

## $\mathrm{p}$-Values: Misused and Misunderstood {#sec-MissUses}



<!-- ### 🧭 What $\mathrm{p}$-Values Tell Us — and What They Don’t {-}

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
## ✅ What $\mathrm{p}$-values do tell us
<br>

* They measure how compatible the data (i.e., the test statistic) are with the null hypothesis $H_0$.

* A small $\mathrm{p}$-value means the observed data (i.e., the test statistic) would be unlikely if $H_0$ were true.

:::

::: {.callout-caution appearance="minimal"}

## 🚫 What $\mathrm{p}$-values do not tell us
<br>

* They do not give the probability that $H_0$ is true or false.

* They do not tell us whether a result is practically important.
::: -->



### 🙁 $\mathrm{p}$-Hacking {-}

$\mathrm{p}$-hacking is arguably the most common misuse of $\mathrm{p}$-values. It happens when researchers keep adjusting their analysis until they find a statistically significant result $(\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} < \alpha)$ — even if there’s no real effect.

🧪 Typical "tricks" include:

* Running lots of tests until one happens to be “significant.”

* Changing the model setup (adding or removing variables) until an insignificant result turns “significant”.

* Selectively including or excluding data points to turn an insignificant result into a “significant” one.

This is called the **multiple comparison problem** — the more tests you run, the higher the chance of finding a false positive (falsely rejecting a correct $H_0$).

---------------------------------------------------------------------

#### **Multiple Comparison Problem** {-}

![Source: [https://xkcd.com/882/](https://xkcd.com/882/)](https://imgs.xkcd.com/comics/significant.png){width=70% fig-align="center"}


::: {.callout-warning  appearance="minimal"}
## ⚠️ Multiple Comparison Problem
<br>
When multiple tests are conducted, the chance of finding at least one “significant” result purely by coincidence increases.

For instance, with $m=20$ **independent** tests at the significance level $\alpha = 0.05$, there is a $64 \%$ chance of incorrectly rejecting at least one null hypothesis:
\begin{align*}
 & P(\text{rejecting $H_0$ in at least one of the $m$ tests}\mid \text{all }H_0\text{'s are true})\\[2ex]
=& 1-P(\text{not rejecting $H_0$ in each of the $m$ tests}\mid \text{all }H_0\text{'s are true})\\[2ex]
=& 1-\left(P(\text{not rejecting $H_0$ in one single test}\mid H_0 \text{ is true})\right)^m\\[2ex]
=& 1-\left(1-P(\text{rejecting $H_0$ in one single test}\mid H_0 \text{ is true})\right)^m\\[2ex]
=& 1-\left(1-P(\text{type I error})\right)^m\\[2ex]
=& 1 - (1-\alpha)^m\\[2ex]
=& 1 - 0.95^{20} \;\approx \; `r round(1 - 0.95^(20), 2)`
\end{align*}
:::

---------------------------------------------------------------------

#### **Adjusting for Multiple Comparisons** {-}

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}

## 🤓 The **Bonferroni Correction** 
<br>
The **Bonferroni Correction** requires using a more stringent significance threshold when multiple tests are performed; namely
$$
\alpha_{\textrm{Bonf}}=\frac{\alpha}{m}
$$ 
for $m$ tests.


\begin{align*}
 & P(\text{rejecting $H_0$ in at least one of the $m$ tests}\mid \text{all }H_0\text{'s are true})\\[2ex]
=& 1 - (1-\alpha_{\textrm{Bonf}})^m\\[2ex]
=& 1 - \left(1-\frac{\alpha}{m}\right)^m\leq \alpha
\end{align*}
For $\alpha = 0.05$ and $m=20\colon$
\begin{align*}
1 - \left(1-\frac{0.05}{20}\right)^{20} &=
1 - \left(1-0.0025\right)^{20} = `r round(1 - (1-0.05/20)^(20), 3)` < 0.05
\end{align*}
:::

Alternatives to the Bonferroni correction:

* Holm–Bonferroni method
* Hochberg's step-up procedure

---------------------------------------------------------------------

#### **Mitigating the Misuse of $\mathrm{p}$-Values** {-}

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
## 🧠 Pre-Registration and 🔁 Replication
<br>

* **Pre-registration:**<br>
Researchers **state their hypotheses and analysis plans *before* looking at the data.**<br>
This reduces the temptation to $\mathrm{p}$-hack and helps distinguish confirmatory from exploratory research.<br>
   * [The Open Science Framework](https://help.osf.io/article/330-welcome-to-registrations)
   * [AsPredicted](https://aspredicted.org/index.php)

<br>

*  **Replication**:<br>
Independent replication studies test whether a finding is robust or simply a statistical fluke (a type I error).
    * [Institute for Replication](https://i4replication.org/)
:::


---------------------------------------------------------------------


### ✅ Correct Interpretation of the $\textrm{p}$-Value {-}

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}

## 🤓 Interpreting Small $\textrm{p}$-Values: $\;\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} < \alpha$
<br>

* **Compatibility with $H_0$:**<br>
A small $\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}$ suggests that the observed statistic $|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|$ is **incompatible** with the null hypothesis $H_0.$ In that case, we may decide that $H_0$ **does not provide a plausible explanation** for the data.

* **Decision Theory:**<br>
When we reject $H_0$ (because $\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} < \alpha$), we **falsely reject** a true $H_0$ (type I error) with probability $\alpha$.<br>
👉 This is why we choose *small* significance levels such as $\alpha = 0.05$ or $\alpha = 0.01.$

* **Statistical Significance ≠ Practical Significance:** <br>
A small $\mathrm{p}$-value does not mean the effect is large or meaningful in practice.<br>
With a very large sample ($n$ large) or low data variability ($\operatorname{Var}(X)$ small), even tiny and unimportant effects will yield very small $\mathrm{p}$-values.


<center> 
📢 A small $\mathrm{p}$-value signals statistical evidence — **not necessarily practical importance**. 
</center>
:::


::: {.callout-warning appearance="minimal"}
## ⚠️ Interpreting Large $\mathrm{p}$-Values: $\;\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} \geq \alpha$
<br>

* **Compatibility with $H_0$:**<br>
A large $\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}$ means the observed test statistic $\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}$ is **compatible** with the null hypothesis $H_0$.<br>
❗️However, this does **not** mean that $H_0$ is true or confirmed.
    * "Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence." [@Sagan_1997].
    * [Argument from ignorance.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argument_from_ignorance)

* **Possible Reasons for Large $\mathrm{p}$-Values:**<br>
Large $\mathrm{p}$-values (even $\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} \approx 1$) can occur when a real effect is simply too small to detect, for example if
   * the **sample size** $n$ is small, or
   * the **data variability** $\operatorname{Var}(X)$ is large.

* **Decision Theory:**<br>
When we **fail to reject** $H_0$ (because $\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} \geq \alpha$), we cannot conclude that $H_0$ is true — only that we do not have enough evidence to reject it. We also do not know the probability of a **type II error** (falsely accepting $H_0$).

<center> 
📢 Statistical tests are designed to **reject** $H_0$ when evidence is strong — not to **prove** that $H_0$ is true. 
</center>

:::

**Last but not least:** 

<center> 
📢 The $\mathrm{p}$-value is **not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.** 
</center>
<br>
The p-value is calculated assuming the null hypothesis is true. Therefore, it cannot be the probability of that same hypothesis being true.


![The Terminator knows stats.](images/terminator.jpeg)


---------------------------------------------------------------

### 📄 Good Practice {-}

Use $\mathrm{p}$-values as one piece of evidence, not the final verdict. Always combine them with 

* effect sizes, 
* confidence intervals, and 
* context.

Accept that there will always be uncertainty, and be **thoughtful, open, and modest.**

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}

* **Be Thoughtful:**
    * Know whether you’re doing an exploratory study (to generate hypotheses) or a more rigidly pre-planned study (to test hypotheses).
    * Invest time and care in sound data collection — good study design and careful execution matter more than fancy statistics.

* **Be Open:**
     * Practice transparency — share your data, methods, and results so others can reproduce your findings.
     * Be honest in communication — “statistical significance” ≠ “scientific importance,” and one study alone rarely proves anything.

* **Be Modest:**
     * Remember: there is no single "true" model — every model is an approximation.
     * Stay humble about what statistical inference can (and cannot) tell us about the real world.
:::


---------------------------------------------------------------

### 📚 The Scientific Debate about $\mathrm{p}$-Values {-}

$\mathrm{p}$-values can be powerful tools — **when used correctly.**
But in practice, they’re often **misused and misinterpreted**, leading to a surprising amount of published **“bad science.”**

This misuse has sparked an ongoing debate:
Should we rely on $\mathrm{p}$-values and the concept of **statistical significance** at all?

📚 **Further reading:**

* [The problem with p Values: How significant are they, really?](https://sciencex.com/wire-news/145707973/the-problem-with-p-values-how-significant-are-they-really.html) [@Cumming_2013]
* [Scientific method: Statistical errors](https://www.nature.com/articles/506150a) [@Nuzzo_2014]
* [Scientists rise up against statistical significance](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-019-00857-9) [@Amrhein_2019] 


To clarify what $\mathrm{p}$-values and **statistical significance** actually mean (and what they don’t), the American Statistical Association (ASA) published two landmark position papers:

📄 **ASA Statements:**

* [The ASA statement on p-values: Context, process, and purpose](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00031305.2016.1154108#d1e167) [@Wasserstein2016asa]
* [Moving to a world beyond "p< 0.05"](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00031305.2019.1583913) [@wasserstein2019asa]
